strengths: The core idea of leveraging Bayesian self-consistency on unlabeled out-of-distribution or real observations to regularize amortized neural posterior estimation is conceptually intuitive and represents a natural semi-supervised extension of self-consistency losses.
The paper is clearly structured, well-written, and transparent about its formulation and current limitations.
The theoretical justification for strict properness (Propositions 1–3) is clean when the likelihood is known.

The parametric ablation study on the multivariate normal model is thorough, investigating dimensions up to 100, unlabeled sample size M, distance of shift, presence of summary networks, and learned versus known likelihoods.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is extremely limited: experiments are confined strictly to a single synthetic multivariate Gaussian mean-estimation toy task. No standard simulation-based inference (SBI) benchmark problems (e.g., SLCP, two moons, Lotka-Volterra, SIR) or real-world datasets are evaluated, despite the paper's core motivation being real-world out-of-simulation robustness.

The submission is explicitly an uncompleted work in progress, as stated on the title page ('This paper is still work in progress. In the full version, we will provide further experiments...'), and falls well short of the standards expected for a complete archival conference paper.

No comparisons against existing robust SBI or domain adaptation baselines are provided (e.g., methods by Gloeckler et al., 2023; Ward et al., 2022; Wehenkel et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023). The method is only compared against vanilla NPE without the self-consistency loss.

The methodological novelty over Schmitt et al. (2024) is modest, as the functional form of the self-consistency variance loss was already established; the primary delta here is evaluating it on unlabeled points x*.

Theoretical guarantees do not hold in the typical likelihood-free SBI setting where the likelihood is also approximated; as acknowledged in the text, joint optimization can admit trivial/degenerate solutions, and empirical results show notable posterior standard deviation bias when the likelihood network is learned.

strengths: Relevant and timely problem: Addressing the failure of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) on out-of-distribution / out-of-simulation observations is a critical open challenge in simulation-based inference.
Principled semi-supervised framing: Leveraging Bayesian self-consistency on unlabeled data provides an elegant way to train posterior estimators without requiring paired ground-truth parameters.
Sound theoretical grounding in the known-likelihood case: Propositions 1–3 clearly demonstrate that the self-consistency loss is strictly proper under an exact likelihood model.

Thorough parametric exploration on the Gaussian benchmark: The case study investigates multiple informative axes, including dimensionality (up to D=100), sample size of unlabeled data, degree of distribution shift, and the inclusion of summary networks.
weaknesses: Incomplete empirical evaluation: The paper acknowledges on the title page that it is a 'work in progress'. Across the entire manuscript, the method is evaluated exclusively on a single toy problem (a conjugate multivariate normal means model). Standard SBI benchmarks (e.g., Lotka-Volterra, SIR, SLCP, Hodgkin-Huxley) and real-world misspecification settings are entirely absent.

Lack of competitive baselines: The proposed method is compared solely against standard NPE without self-consistency. There are no comparisons against existing robustness/adaptation techniques for ABI discussed in Section 3 (e.g., Wehenkel et al., 2024; Ward et al., 2022; Gloeckler et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023).

Fundamental limitation when likelihood is unknown: Amortized inference is primarily motivated by likelihood-free / simulator-based settings. However, when the likelihood is approximated, strict properness no longer holds (as acknowledged in Section 2.3), and the empirical results in Figure 3 exhibit noticeable degradation, particularly in posterior variance estimation.

Limited novelty over prior work: The self-consistency loss formulation itself was introduced by Schmitt et al. (ICML 2024). The main conceptual contribution here is applying it to unlabeled out-of-distribution samples, but the methodology remains closely tied to the existing framework.

strengths: The core idea of incorporating unlabeled observations via Bayesian self-consistency into amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) to tackle out-of-distribution / misspecification issues is natural and conceptually appealing.
The paper is clearly written, well-structured, and easy to follow.

The parameter sensitivity study on the multivariate Gaussian case (investigating dimensionality, sample size of unlabeled points, and magnitude of shift) is conducted systematically and clearly illustrated.
weaknesses: Severely incomplete empirical validation: The manuscript explicitly describes itself as a 'work in progress' and 'proof-of-concept' (see abstract and page 1 footnote). It only evaluates a single, toy linear-Gaussian problem (normal means). Standard benchmark tasks in simulation-based inference (e.g., SLCP, SIR, Lotka-Volterra, or real scientific simulators) are completely missing.

Limited novelty over prior work: The log-variance self-consistency loss was already introduced by Schmitt et al. (ICML 2024). Evaluating this loss on unlabeled samples is a straightforward extension, and the mathematical proofs (Propositions 1–4) are elementary rearrangements of Bayes' theorem.

Weak justification for the primary SBI setting: The main selling point of amortized simulation-based inference is performing posterior estimation when the likelihood is intractable. When the likelihood is known analytically, standard sampling or variational tools are usually available. When the likelihood is unknown and must be estimated jointly, the theoretical guarantees of strict properness no longer hold (as acknowledged by the authors), and empirical results in Figure 3 show noticeable degradation (especially posterior SD bias).

Disproportionate claims: The paper claims in both the abstract and discussion that the method represents a 'major breakthrough in neural ABI', which is inappropriate and unsupported given only synthetic Gaussian toy experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses a very important and timely problem in simulation-based inference (SBI) and amortized Bayesian inference (ABI): failure to generalize under domain shifts, out-of-simulation observations, and model misspecification.
Formulating the use of self-consistency losses on unlabeled out-of-distribution / real-world data as semi-supervised amortized inference is conceptually elegant and intuitive.
Theoretical properties (strict properness of the self-consistency loss and the composite semi-supervised loss when the likelihood is known) are clearly stated and proved in the appendix.

The empirical ablation study on the multivariate normal model is thorough, investigating dimensions (up to D=100), sample size of unlabeled data, degree of distribution shift, presence of summary networks, and estimated vs. known likelihoods.
weaknesses: Lack of empirical comparisons with existing robust SBI baselines: The paper thoroughly discusses related work on robustness in ABI (e.g., Gloeckler et al., 2023; Ward et al., 2022; Siahkoohi et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023; Wehenkel et al., 2024), but the experimental sections only compare standard NPE against NPE + SC. Without benchmarking against existing mitigation or calibration techniques, it is difficult to quantify the practical advantage over alternative approaches.

Reliance on tractable / known likelihoods: The theoretical guarantees (Propositions 1–3) strictly require a known likelihood p(x | theta). However, SBI is primarily motivated by settings where the likelihood is intractable (likelihood-free). When the likelihood is estimated via a surrogate q(x | theta), the properness guarantee breaks down, and the empirical results (Figure 4, top row) show noticeable deterioration in posterior variance calibration (posterior SD bias).

Limited complexity of experimental benchmarks: The empirical validation is restricted to two relatively simple models (a multivariate Gaussian means model and a linear ARX(1) model), both featuring tractable Gaussian likelihoods. Evaluating on established, higher-complexity scientific simulator benchmarks (e.g., standard SBI benchmark tasks with synthetic or real misspecification) would significantly strengthen the paper.

Overstated claims: Describing the proposed method as a 'major breakthrough in neural ABI' (both in the Abstract and Discussion) is overly bold given that evaluation is limited to two low-complexity models with known Gaussian likelihoods and lacks empirical comparison to existing robust SBI methods.

strengths: The conceptual formulation of leveraging Bayesian self-consistency on unlabeled real-world or out-of-simulation data is elegant and addresses a major failure mode of amortized Bayesian inference (poor generalization under distribution shift/misspecification).
The paper is clearly structured and well-written, with straightforward theoretical propositions establishing the strict properness of the composite semi-supervised objective.

The empirical results on the multivariate normal benchmark provide clear intuition on how self-consistency prevents the typical posterior collapse and bias observed in standard neural posterior estimation (NPE).

The application to real-world European air passenger traffic data effectively demonstrates that incorporating unlabeled data from a subset of countries can align amortized estimates closely with gold-standard MCMC (Stan) without requiring post-hoc sampling.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on tractable likelihoods: The core motivation for simulation-based inference (SBI) is typically to perform Bayesian inference when the likelihood is intractable. In the paper's experiments (multivariate normal and AR(1)), the likelihood is known analytically. While the appendix explores a learned likelihood network, performance drops noticeably and the theoretical guarantees of strict properness no longer hold without additional constraints (as noted by the authors). This limits the current applicability to broader likelihood-free SBI problems.

Lack of empirical comparisons with existing robust SBI baselines: While the related work cites several recent methods for robust amortized inference (e.g., Gloeckler et al., 2023; Ward et al., 2022; Wehenkel et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2023), none of these methods are included as empirical baselines. The paper only benchmarks against standard unaugmented NPE.

Limited diversity and complexity of experimental benchmarks: The empirical evaluation is restricted to two relatively simple Gaussian-noise models (a normal means problem and an AR(1) linear regression model). Evaluating the approach on standard scientific benchmark simulators (e.g., Lotka-Volterra, SIR, or Hodgkin-Huxley) under controlled misspecification would provide much stronger evidence for the method's real-world utility.

Overstated claims: Calling the method a 'major breakthrough in neural ABI' in both the abstract and discussion seems disproportionate given the reliance on known likelihoods, the existing literature on self-consistency losses (Schmitt et al., 2024), and the narrow experimental scope.

strengths: Principled and intuitive framework: The paper proposes a neat and theoretically grounded semi-supervised formulation for Amortized Bayesian Inference (ABI) by leveraging Bayesian self-consistency on unlabeled out-of-distribution/real-world observations.

Theoretical soundness: Propositions 1–3 rigorously establish that the Bayesian self-consistency ratio loss is strictly proper, confirming that adding unlabeled data does not introduce an asymptotic bias or negative trade-off against the standard simulation-based loss under the true posterior.
Clear presentation: The paper is well-structured and written with clarity, providing intuitive motivation and transparent details regarding training setups in the appendix.

Compelling synthetic demonstration: The multivariate Gaussian experiment effectively illustrates a major failure mode of standard NPE (severe posterior variance collapse and mean shift when data shifts away from the prior) and convincingly demonstrates how NPE with self-consistency (NPE+SC) mitigates this issue.
weaknesses: Lack of comparisons against robust ABI baselines: The paper thoroughly discusses related work on robust ABI (e.g., Ward et al., 2022; Gloeckler et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023; Wehenkel et al., 2024), yet the empirical evaluation exclusively benchmarks against standard unregularized NPE and MCMC (Stan). Demonstrating that the proposed approach outperforms or offers a better accuracy/amortization trade-off than existing robustness mechanisms is critical.

Dependence on tractable likelihoods in an SBI context: A primary motivation for simulation-based inference (SBI) is handling models with intractable likelihoods. The strongest theoretical and empirical results in the paper rely on an analytical likelihood $p(x | \theta)$. When the likelihood must be approximated by a neural network, Proposition 1 no longer strictly guarantees correctness (as noted in Section 2.3), and the empirical results in Appendix A.3 show noticeable degradation (e.g., bias in posterior standard deviations).

Limited diversity and complexity of benchmarks: The empirical validation is restricted to two relatively simple problems (a conjugate multivariate normal model and a linear autoregressive AR(1) model with additive Gaussian noise). Evaluating on standard nonlinear/mechanistic SBI benchmarks with complex simulation dynamics (e.g., Lotka-Volterra, SIR, or Hodgkin-Huxley under misspecification) would significantly strengthen the empirical backing.

Missing analysis on hyperparameter sensitivity and training stability: The loss weight $\lambda$ and the proposal distribution $p_C(\theta)$ (sampling from $q_t(\theta | x^*)$) are critical to the training dynamics. There is little discussion or empirical sensitivity analysis exploring how different choices of $\lambda$ affect performance or whether the self-consistency variance objective induces optimization instability early in training.

Overstated claims: Assertions such as claiming the method 'represents a major breakthrough in neural ABI' (Abstract and Discussion) are premature given the limited benchmark variety and the absence of comparisons against competing robust inference methods.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and pervasive challenge in amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) and simulation-based inference (SBI): posterior collapse and extreme bias when conditioning on out-of-distribution or misspecified data.
The formulation of semi-supervised ABI leveraging Bayesian self-consistency on unlabeled observations is intuitive, elegant, and theoretically sound, with established strict properness guarantees.

The empirical evaluation is diverse and thorough, spanning controllable Gaussian benchmarks across varying dimensions, a real-world econometric model benchmarked against Stan MCMC, a biophysical Hodgkin-Huxley ODE system, and high-dimensional MNIST image denoising.
The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and the empirical findings convincingly show substantial robustness gains even when trained on very few unlabeled observations.
weaknesses: A key limitation of the self-consistency approach is the requirement of an evaluable likelihood $p(x|\theta)$. While the authors test a neural likelihood estimator $q(x|\theta)$ (NPLE) when the likelihood is intractable, Proposition 4 notes that strict properness is lost when both likelihood and posterior are approximate, and empirical results indicate increased bias in posterior variance. A deeper analysis of the failure modes or stability under severe likelihood approximation error would strengthen the work.

The empirical evaluation lacks direct comparison against existing robust SBI or domain adaptation methods (e.g., scoring rule-based generalized Bayesian inference, MMD-based SBI, or unsupervised domain adaptation techniques mentioned in related work). The benchmarks primarily compare NPE/NPLE against NPE/NPLE + SC.

The paper provides limited analysis on the sensitivity and tuning of key hyperparameters, notably the trade-off weight $\lambda$ in Eq. (2) and the choice/dynamics of the proposal distribution $p_C(\theta)$ used to estimate the consistency loss.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-recognized failure mode of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI): brittleness and bias under simulation gaps, out-of-distribution observations, and model misspecification.

Presents a principled semi-supervised formulation that leverages Bayesian self-consistency to guide the neural posterior estimator on unlabeled observations (e.g., real-world data) without requiring ground-truth parameter labels.

Provides solid theoretical grounding showing that Bayesian self-consistency losses based on likelihood-to-posterior ratios are strictly proper scoring rules under known likelihoods (Propositions 1-3).

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse domains, including an analytical multivariate normal model, real-world economic time series benchmarked against Stan MCMC, a biophysical dynamical system (Hodgkin-Huxley), and high-dimensional image denoising on MNIST.
Maintains full amortization at inference time, avoiding the heavy computational cost of post-hoc test-time MCMC or iterative optimization.
weaknesses: Lack of empirical comparisons with existing robust simulation-based inference (SBI) baselines: While Section 3 mentions prior work on misspecification and robustness (e.g., Gloeckler et al., 2023; Ward et al., 2022; Wehenkel et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023), the experiments solely compare the proposed method (NPE + SC) against vanilla NPE and reference posterior samplers.

Reliance on tractable or well-estimated likelihoods: The theoretical guarantees (strict properness) rely on having access to the true likelihood function. For true likelihood-free settings where likelihoods must be approximated simultaneously (e.g., NPLE), strict properness does not hold and trivial solutions exist (Section 2.3). The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of when and how joint neural likelihood-posterior learning might degenerate or fail.

Sensitivity and training stability details: In Eq. (4), sampling parameters from the proposal distribution $p_C(\theta)$ (such as the current posterior estimate $q_t$) introduces gradient variance and potential optimization instability. A more detailed sensitivity analysis regarding consistency sample size $L$, loss weight $\lambda$, and schedule ramping would strengthen the practical utility of the method.

Conceptual distinction in the unlabeled data generation: In the Hodgkin-Huxley experiment, the 'unlabeled' data is simulated from an expanded synthetic parameter distribution rather than sourced from real observations, which aligns more closely with broad-prior simulation without labels than true semi-supervised learning on empirical data.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) often suffers catastrophic failure and variance collapse when confronted with out-of-distribution or misspecified data. Addressing this simulation gap is crucial for practical adoption.

Principled semi-supervised formulation: Leveraging Bayesian self-consistency on unlabeled observations $x^*$ provides a natural mechanism to incorporate observed real-world data without requiring ground-truth parameter labels $\theta^*$.

Theoretical support: The paper provides clear propositions establishing that the self-consistency variance loss is strictly proper when the likelihood is known, guaranteeing that optimizing the semi-supervised objective does not distort the target posterior.

Diverse application domains: The method is validated across multiple distinct domains, including a synthetic normal model across varying dimensions, econometric time-series (air passenger traffic benchmarked against Stan MCMC), biophysical ODE systems (Hodgkin-Huxley), and image denoising.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty over Schmitt et al. (2024): The core mathematical loss—penalizing the variance of the log Bayesian self-consistency ratio $\log p(x|\theta) + \log p(\theta) - \log q(\theta|x)$—was originally formulated by Schmitt et al. (ICML 2024). Applying this loss to unlabeled data points $x^*$ in a semi-supervised setup is a straightforward extension of their framework.

Lack of competitive robust SBI baselines: While the related work section highlights several recent robust ABI / simulation-based inference methods (e.g., adversarial regularization by Gloeckler et al., 2023; calibration methods by Wehenkel et al., 2024; MMD/scoring-rule approaches; and unsupervised domain adaptation as discussed by Elsemüller et al., 2025), none of these techniques are empirically compared against. The experiments exclusively compare standard NPE against NPE + SC.

Tension with the likelihood-free setting: A primary motivation of ABI is performing inference when the likelihood is intractable. When the likelihood must be approximated with a neural network $q(x|\theta)$ (NPLE), the self-consistency loss is no longer strictly proper on its own (as acknowledged in Section 2.3). The empirical results in Figure 7 (top row) indicate noticeable bias in the posterior standard deviation under estimated likelihoods, weakening the robustness claims in truly likelihood-free regimes.

Evaluation in high-dimensional tasks lacks quantitative rigor: In the MNIST denoising experiment (Section 4.4), the evaluation relies almost entirely on qualitative inspections of reconstructed means and pixel variance maps. Standard quantitative image inverse problem metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, log-likelihood, coverage/calibration metrics across the test set) are omitted.

Sensitivity to proposal distribution and training dynamics: Optimizing the variance over $\theta \sim q_t(\theta|x^*)$ when $x^*$ is heavily out-of-distribution can induce high variance or instability early in training. While the paper mentions annealing the loss weight for MNIST, a systematic sensitivity analysis regarding the choice of $p_C(\theta)$, batch sizes, and consistency samples $L$ is missing.

strengths: Principled and elegant framework: The paper provides a well-motivated semi-supervised extension to amortized Bayesian inference (ABI). By leveraging Bayesian self-consistency properties as strictly proper scoring rules on unlabeled observations, it targets the exact analytic posterior without introducing regularizers that distort the Bayesian target distribution.

Practicality of the semi-supervised setting: Unlike existing approaches that require ground-truth parameter labels for real observations or post-hoc sampling corrections (e.g., MCMC/SVI) that destroy amortization, this approach only requires unlabeled observations from the deployment domain during training.

Compelling and comprehensive empirical validation: The method is evaluated across diverse domains—multivariate Gaussians up to 100 dimensions, a real-world econometric/air traffic time series compared directly against Stan HMC, a biophysical Hodgkin-Huxley model, and an image denoising task. The results consistently demonstrate substantial improvements in robustness with very few unlabeled samples (e.g., M as low as 4).

Thorough comparisons: The authors provide meaningful comparisons against standard NPE, domain adaptation methods (NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN), NNPE, VAEs, and previous fully supervised self-consistency methods.
High clarity and presentation quality: The paper is clearly structured, well written, and supported by extensive details and ablations in the appendices.
weaknesses: Reliance on tractable or known likelihoods: The strongest theoretical properties and empirical gains rely on the availability of an explicit likelihood function $p(x | \theta)$. When the likelihood itself is unknown and parameterized via a neural approximator (joint NPLE), joint properness is no longer guaranteed and empirical performance degrades (as shown by standard deviation bias in Section 4.1).

Computational overhead during training: Computing the self-consistency loss requires drawing $L$ parameter samples from the flow and evaluating both log-posterior and log-likelihood densities at each iteration. This limits compatibility with continuous-time normalizing flows or diffusion models where density evaluation requires expensive numerical ODE integration.

Training stability and sensitivity to scheduling: As acknowledged by the authors, SC losses can suffer from gradient instabilities early in training when the posterior approximation is poor. While a linear warm-up schedule for $\lambda$ is utilized, deeper analysis or sensitivity ablations regarding the choice of $L$ and the warm-up schedule across complex tasks would be valuable.

strengths: Principled and elegant formulation: The paper introduces a semi-supervised framework for amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) that incorporates unlabeled empirical/real data via Bayesian self-consistency losses. This directly addresses the critical fragility of neural posterior estimators under simulation gaps and model misspecification without requiring ground-truth parameter labels for real data.

Theoretical soundness: Propositions 1–3 demonstrate that the self-consistency loss is strictly proper and targets the exact analytic posterior of the specified model. Unlike unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) or heuristic regularizers that perturb the target posterior, the proposed objective introduces no trade-off with the supervised simulation loss at the global optimum.

Comprehensive and diverse empirical evaluation: The method is validated across a wide spectrum of tasks, including a controlled multivariate normal benchmark (up to D=100), real-world economic time-series forecasting (air passenger traffic validated against gold-standard Stan MCMC), a biophysical differential equation model (Hodgkin-Huxley), and high-dimensional Bayesian image denoising (MNIST).

Strong benchmarking: The paper thoroughly evaluates against relevant baselines and competing robustness paradigms, including standard NPE, online NPE, Schmitt et al. (2024), VAEs, as well as domain-adaptation approaches (NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, NNPE).

High quality of presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is well-structured, clearly written, includes complete proofs in the appendix, and provides concrete architectural, optimization, and hardware details.
weaknesses: Dependence on tractable or surrogate likelihoods: Evaluating the self-consistency ratio requires computing the likelihood $p(x^*|\theta)$. For true simulation-based / likelihood-free settings where the likelihood density is unavailable, one must train a neural likelihood estimator $q(x|\theta)$. As shown in Figure 7 (top row), when the likelihood is estimated, posterior standard deviation bias and MMD increase noticeably compared to the known likelihood setting.

Training dynamics and optimization stability: As noted in Appendix B, self-consistency loss is prone to numerical instability and gradient explosion early in training when posterior approximations are poor, necessitating specific scheduling strategies for the consistency weight $\lambda$. A more detailed sensitivity analysis regarding the schedule of $\lambda$ and number of consistency samples $L$ in the main text would be beneficial.

Gradient flow through the proposal distribution: In Equation (4), the expectation/variance is taken with respect to the current approximate posterior $\theta \sim q_t(\theta | h(x^*))$. It should be made explicit in the text whether gradients are propagated through the sampling mechanism (e.g., pathwise derivative via reparameterization) or whether the proposal is treated as a detached proposal distribution (score-function / stop-gradient).

strengths: Sound and elegant formulation: Extending Bayesian self-consistency (SC) to an unsupervised/semi-supervised setting by leveraging unlabeled observations without requiring ground-truth parameters is a clever and conceptually sound idea to tackle the out-of-simulation/misspecification gap in amortized Bayesian inference (ABI).

Solid theoretical foundation: The authors prove that the Bayesian self-consistency loss is strictly proper (Propositions 1-3) and targets the true analytic posterior under the assumed model without introducing ad-hoc regularization or altering the target distribution, irrespective of the unlabeled data distribution p*(x).

Preservation of amortization: Unlike post-hoc MCMC corrections, generalized Bayesian inference, or test-time optimization methods, this approach maintains the ultra-fast amortized inference capabilities of neural posterior estimation at test time.

Comprehensive and diverse empirical evaluation: The method is validated on a spectrum of benchmarks ranging from controlled multivariate Gaussians (up to 100 dimensions) to real-world econometric time series (Eurostat air traffic evaluated against Stan MCMC), high-dimensional biophysical ODE models (Hodgkin-Huxley), and image denoising on MNIST.

Thorough benchmarking and ablations: The appendix provides extensive comparisons against relevant baselines, including unsupervised domain adaptation methods (NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD), NNPE, VAEs, and supervised SC variants, as well as ablations on sample size M, dimensionality, and summary networks.
weaknesses: Dependence on tractable densities: Because the variance loss relies on pointwise log-density evaluation of q(theta | x) (and p(x | theta) when known), the framework is largely constrained to normalizing flows (e.g., neural spline flows). It cannot be directly or efficiently applied to score-based diffusion models or free-form flow matching without computationally expensive numerical ODE integration.

Degradation when the likelihood is intractable/estimated: When the likelihood must also be approximated jointly (NPLE), Proposition 4 clarifies that joint strict properness is lost without additional constraints, and empirical results (Section 4.1 / Appendix D) indicate noticeable bias in posterior variance compared to the known-likelihood setting.

Heuristic scheduling of the consistency weight: For higher-dimensional problems (e.g., MNIST), the loss can suffer from early optimization instabilities, necessitating a warm-up schedule for lambda. Guidance on how to choose or tune this schedule for novel problems without ground truth remains heuristic.

Placement of key baseline comparisons: Several critical baseline comparisons (such as NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD, NNPE, and VAE) are deferred to Appendices D.1 and F.1; integrating a summarized quantitative table directly into the main text would strengthen the presentation.
